newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FOCUS-Bulgarian lev steadies after big fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bulgarian lev steadies after big fall.

text.p: The Bulgarian lev steadied on Friday after falling about 30 percent on the week as Bulgarians rushed to convert their savings into dollars.
Interbank trade was light ahead of a central bank board meeting.

The lev firmed to 340-360 per dollar in early trade from 390-395 at Thursday's close. Dealers said the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) was not seen intervening in the market. The lev started the week at 272-275.

Loss of confidence in the lev and rumours about the likely impact of a currency board, proposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to stabilise the economy, sparked panic this week. On Thursday alone the lev fell 18 percent.
Some 75 percent of SSB deposits are invested in Treasury paper, and depositors feared the finance ministry might suspend payments on government securities under a currency board.
Bulgarians besieged the State Savings Bank, the country's biggest savings institution, withdrawing more than 14 billion levs since last week.
BNB governor Lyubomir Filipov said on Wednesday his bank would continue to support the lev as much as it could but it could not deplete its reserves to counter a highly speculative dollar rush.
"They (BNB) may leave the market free for a few weeks ahead of introduction of a currency board," said one dealer. He did not expect the lev to fall below 400 to the dollar next week.
Politicians and bankers are discussing the currency board scheme which could stabilise the economy by forcing Bulgaria to match levs in circulation with foreign exchange reserves.
Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economic Development Roumen Gechev said the exchange rate was the central bank's problem and not the government's responsibility.

"According to the constitution and the central bank's statutes, responsibility for the foreign exchange market is borne by the central bank. We have too many responsibilities to take care of the exchange rate as well."
The central bank board adjourned its regular weekly meeting on Thursday evening and was due to meet again later on Friday to discuss the crisis.

"The ghost of hyperinflation started to haunt Bulgaria this week," Trade Minister Anastas Paparizov told Kontinent newspaper. Inflation was at a monthly 16.7 percent in October and totalled 195.1 percent since the beginning of the year.
He said the IMF proposal for a currency board was not enough to save the economy and Bulgaria should seek a rescheduling of its debt to the Paris Club of government creditors.

Payments of $300 million on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt fall due in the first quarter of 1997 and debt markets speculate that Bulgaria could become the first country to default on a Brady debt restructuring deal.
"The national currency, the lev, died yesterday," said the Socialist party daily Douma, renewing its accusations of a foreign conspiracy to destroy the economy.
"According to experts, the rise of the dollar was triggered by ING and Raiffeisenbank which were especially active in buying up foreign currency during the whole day," it said.
The banks denied the accusation. One spokesman said: "We had no impact on the market yesterday."
BNB foreign exchange reserves stood near $541 million at the end of October, down from $1.434 billion a year ago. The central bank also manages gold reserves worth some $400 million.
